Sofia kicked the soccer ball as hard as she could. It sailed over the fence, and landed directly on Mr. Okafor's front porch, where something shattered with a terrible crash.

She raced to the fence and peeked over. Mr. Okafor's favorite blue flowerpot lay in pieces on the steps, and dirt and red petals were scattered everywhere. Her ball rested quietly beside the broken pot, as if it had done nothing wrong.

Sofia looked up and down the street. Nobody was outside. His car was gone, so he was probably at work. She realized that she could grab the ball, hurry home, and no one would ever discover what had happened.

She climbed over the fence, picked up the ball, and returned to her own yard. That evening, however, she could not stop thinking about the broken pot. At dinner, she pushed her vegetables around her plate, and in bed she stared at the ceiling for hours. Mr. Okafor waved to her every morning when she walked to the bus stop and always asked about her games. How could she wave back tomorrow and pretend that everything was normal?

The next afternoon, Sofia emptied her piggy bank onto her bed and counted eleven dollars and forty cents. Then she took a deep breath and walked next door.

Mr. Okafor was sweeping the steps when she arrived, and Sofia's heart pounded like a drum. "I'm the one who broke your flowerpot," she said quickly. "It was my soccer ball, and I'm really sorry, so I want to pay for a new one." She held out the coins and bills.

Mr. Okafor leaned on his broom and studied her for a long moment before he smiled. "That old pot was older than you are," he said. "Keep your money, but I do have a job for you, because those flowers still need a home."

On Saturday, Sofia and Mr. Okafor drove to the hardware store and selected a new pot. Back at his house, they filled it with fresh soil and replanted the flowers that had survived. Sofia's hands were muddy, but she felt lighter than she had in days.

"You know," Mr. Okafor said as they watered the pot, "plenty of people would have stayed silent, and telling the truth takes real courage."

Sofia grinned. From then on, she practiced her powerful kicks at the park.

choices: Soccer is a game that should only be played at school.
Telling the truth can be hard, but it is the right thing to do.
Money is the best way to fix any mistake.
Neighbors should always keep a tall fence between their yards.
explanation: Sofia is tempted to hide what she did, but she confesses, and Mr. Okafor praises her courage. The story shows that telling the truth is right even when it is hard.

passage:
Imagine you are walking through a forest. A brown moth rests on a tree trunk right in front of you, but you walk past without seeing it. The moth is not invisible. It simply blends in with the bark. This is called camouflage, and it is one of the most useful tools an animal can have.

Camouflage helps animals survive. Many animals are hunted by others. If a hungry bird cannot see a moth, it cannot eat the moth. Camouflage also helps hunters. A tiger's orange and black stripes look bright in a zoo, but in tall, dry grass they break up the tiger's shape. Deer and other animals may not notice the tiger until it is too late.

Some animals match the color of their home. A polar bear's white fur blends in with snow and ice. A flounder is a flat fish that lies on the sandy ocean floor. Its spotted brown skin looks just like the sand around it.

Other animals change their color with the seasons. In summer, the arctic fox has brown and gray fur that matches rocks and plants. When winter comes, it grows thick white fur that matches the snow.

A few animals can change color very quickly. An octopus can change both the color and the bumpy texture of its skin in less than a second. One moment it looks like a rock covered in seaweed, and the next moment it seems to disappear into the coral.

Some insects hide by copying the shape of things around them. A walking stick insect is long, thin, and brown. When it holds still on a branch, it looks just like a twig. Leaf insects are flat and green, with markings that look like the veins of a real leaf.

Not every animal tries to hide, though. Some animals copy the colors of dangerous animals instead. The scarlet kingsnake is harmless, but its red, black, and yellow bands look a lot like those of the coral snake, which is very poisonous. Many predators stay away from both snakes.

Scientists are still discovering new examples of camouflage. Whether an animal is hiding from a hunter or sneaking up on its next meal, blending in can mean the difference between life and death.

explanation: The passage gives many examples of animals that hide by matching colors, changing colors, or copying shapes, all to help them survive.

passage:
Long ago, when the world was new, the nights were completely dark. There was no moon, and there were no stars. When the sun went down, the animals of the forest stayed close to their homes, because anyone who wandered away in the darkness could easily get lost.

In those days, Firefly was a plain brown beetle. She was so small that the other animals hardly noticed her. Owl had his sharp eyes, Fox had her clever nose, and Bear had his great strength. Firefly had nothing special at all, or so everyone said.

One evening, a young rabbit named Pip hopped too far from his burrow while chasing a butterfly. Before he knew it, the sun had disappeared, and Pip could not even see his own paws. Frightened and alone, he sat under a fern and began to cry.

The animals heard him, but no one knew how to help. "I can see a little in the dark," said Owl, "but I cannot lead him through the thick bushes." Fox sniffed the air. "I can smell him, but the wind keeps changing." Bear only shook his heavy head.

Firefly listened from a blade of grass. She was tiny, but she was not afraid, so she flew up and up to the great Sky Spirit, who kept the light of the sun in a golden bowl.

"Please," Firefly begged, "give me a small piece of light so I can bring Pip home."

The Sky Spirit studied the little beetle. "Many large animals have asked me for light so that they could show off," it said. "You are the first to ask for light to help someone else." It dipped a finger into the bowl and touched Firefly's tail. At once, her tail glowed a soft yellow-green.

Firefly zipped down through the trees, flashing her new light. Pip looked up and saw a bright spark dancing in front of him. He followed it over roots and around rocks until he reached his family's burrow. His mother hugged him tightly.

From that night on, the other animals never ignored Firefly again. And to this day, on warm summer nights, fireflies flash their lights over fields and forests. People say they are still looking for anyone who has lost the way home.
stem: What does this story mainly try to explain?
choices: why owls can see in the dark
why the sun sets every night
explanation: The Sky Spirit makes Firefly's tail glow, and the story says fireflies still flash their lights today. It is a tale that explains why fireflies glow.

On a small island in New York Harbor, a giant green lady holds a torch high above the water. She is the Statue of Liberty. For more than a hundred years, she has welcomed ships into the harbor. But few people know how hard it was to build her.

The idea began in France in 1865. Some French people liked the way the United States stood for freedom. They wanted to give Americans a gift. It would mark one hundred years since the Declaration of Independence. A young artist named Auguste Bartholdi agreed to design a huge statue of a woman with a torch.

Building the statue took many years. Workers hammered thin sheets of copper into shape by hand. The copper skin is only about as thick as two pennies, so it could not stand up on its own. A builder named Gustave Eiffel planned a strong iron frame to hold it up from the inside. Later, Eiffel built a famous tall tower in Paris.

The French agreed to pay for the statue. Americans agreed to build the stone base, called a pedestal. But it was hard to raise money for the pedestal, and for a while, work stopped. Then a newspaper owner named Joseph Pulitzer asked his readers for help. He promised to print the name of every person who gave money, no matter how small the gift. More than 120,000 people sent money. Many of them, including children, gave less than one dollar.

In 1885, the statue was taken apart and shipped across the ocean in 214 wooden crates. Workers put the pieces back together on top of the new base. On October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was at last shown to the world.

passage:
In the fall of 1886, eleven-year-old Ellie Hart lived with her father on a tiny, rocky island off the coast of Maine. The only building on the island was a white lighthouse. Every evening, Papa climbed the winding stairs to the top of the tower and lit the great lamp. Its beam swept across the dark water and warned ships to stay away from the dangerous rocks.

Ellie understood every part of the job. She helped Papa polish the enormous glass lens until it sparkled, and she trimmed the wicks and carried heavy cans of oil up all ninety-two steps. Still, Papa always lit the lamp himself.

One gray November afternoon, Papa rowed to the mainland to buy flour and lamp oil. "I'll be back before dark," he promised. But an hour later, the wind began to howl. Rain lashed the windows, and huge waves crashed over the rocks. Ellie watched the harbor, but she saw no sign of Papa's small boat. He could not row back in a storm like this.

As the sky grew darker, Ellie's stomach twisted. Somewhere out on the ocean, ships were sailing toward the island. Without the light, they might crash into the rocks.

Ellie grabbed a lantern and climbed the stairs. The tower shook with every gust. At the top, she struck a match with trembling fingers. The first match blew out, and so did the second. On the third attempt, the wick caught, and the great lamp blazed to life. Its beam stretched across the stormy sea.

All night long, Ellie stayed awake in the tower. Every few hours, she carried up more oil and trimmed the wick so the flame would stay bright. Once, through the rain, she spotted the lights of a ship. She held her breath as it turned slowly away from the rocks and sailed safely past.

At sunrise, the storm finally ended, and Ellie noticed a small boat rowing toward the island. Papa leaped onto the dock and ran up the path.

"I saw the light burning all night from the mainland," he said, hugging her. "I knew it had to be you."

Ellie was exhausted, but she smiled. That evening, Papa handed her the box of matches. "Tonight," he said, "you light the lamp."

passage:
Deep beneath your feet, Earth is very hot. Most of the time, you cannot feel that heat. But in some places, it bursts out through the ground in a volcano.

Earth is made of layers. The outer layer, called the crust, is a thin shell of solid rock. It is broken into giant pieces called plates, which fit together like a puzzle. Under the crust is the mantle. In some places, rock deep in the mantle melts. This melted rock is called magma.

Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It collects in a pool called a magma chamber, a few miles below the surface. Gas bubbles in the magma build up pressure, much like the bubbles in a shaken bottle of soda. When the pressure becomes too great, the magma pushes up through cracks in the crust and bursts out. This is called an eruption. Once magma reaches the surface, it has a new name: lava.

Not all eruptions are the same. Some volcanoes, like the ones in Hawaii, have runny lava that flows gently out of the ground. People can sometimes stand at a safe distance and watch glowing rivers of lava move downhill. Other volcanoes have thick, sticky magma that traps gas. When these volcanoes erupt, they explode violently. They can blast ash and rock miles into the sky. In 1980, Mount St. Helens in Washington State erupted this way. The blast knocked down forests for miles around.

Over time, layers of cooled lava and ash pile up around the opening. Layer by layer, they build a mountain. Some volcanoes grow very tall. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises more than 33,000 feet from the ocean floor. Measured from its base, it is taller than Mount Everest.

Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help people. Volcanic ash breaks down into rich soil that is good for growing crops. Many islands, including all of the Hawaiian Islands, were formed by volcanoes.

Scientists who study volcanoes are called volcanologists. They use special tools to measure small earthquakes, changes in the shape of the ground, and gases coming from a volcano. These signs can warn that an eruption may be coming soon. With enough warning, people who live nearby can move to safety.

These signs can warn that an eruption may be coming soon. With enough warning, people who live nearby can move to safety.

stem: The prefix DIS- in "dishonest" and "disagree" means
explanation: DIS- means not or the opposite of. Dishonest means not honest, and disagree means the opposite of agree.

stem: The prefix OVER- in "overcook" and "oversleep" means
explanation: OVER- means too much. To overcook food is to cook it too much, and to oversleep is to sleep too long.

stem: The suffix -NESS in "kindness" and "darkness" means
explanation: -NESS turns an adjective into a noun meaning the state of being. Kindness is the state of being kind.

stem: The suffix -LY in "quickly" and "softly" means
explanation: -LY makes an adverb that tells how something is done. Quickly means in a quick way.

stem: The root TRACT in "tractor" and "subtract" means
explanation: TRACT means to pull. A tractor pulls heavy loads, and to subtract is to take away, or pull out, a number.

stem: The root PED in "pedal" and "pedestrian" means
explanation: PED means foot. You push a pedal with your foot, and a pedestrian is a person traveling on foot.

stem: The prefix TRI- in "triangle" and "tricycle" means
explanation: TRI- means three. A triangle has three angles, and a tricycle has three wheels.

stem: The prefix MID- in "midnight" and "midweek" means
explanation: MID- means middle. Midnight is the middle of the night, and midweek is the middle of the week.

stem: The root JECT in "eject" and "reject" means
explanation: JECT means to throw. To eject is to throw out, and to reject is to throw back or refuse.

stem: The root GEO in "geography" and "geode" means
explanation: GEO means earth. Geography is the study of Earth's land and places.

stem:
The hallway was so CRAMMED with students that I could barely squeeze through.

What does CRAMMED mean?
explanation: If you can barely squeeze through, the hallway must be completely full of students.

stem:
Jamal's legs ached, but he was DETERMINED to finish the race, so he kept running.

What does DETERMINED mean?
choices: firmly decided not to give up
explanation: Jamal keeps running even though his legs ache, which shows he has firmly decided not to give up.

stem:
The magician waved his hand, and the coin seemed to VANISH into thin air.

Which word means the SAME as VANISH?
explanation: Something that vanishes "into thin air" can no longer be seen, so vanish means disappear.

stem:
Choose the word that means the OPPOSITE of FORTUNATE.

We were FORTUNATE that the rain stopped just before the parade began.
explanation: Fortunate means lucky. Its opposite is unlucky.

stem:
Choose the word that means the OPPOSITE of CAUTIOUS.

The CAUTIOUS driver slowed down on the icy road.
explanation: A cautious person is careful to avoid danger. The opposite is careless.

stem:
Maya CONCEALED the birthday present under her bed so her brother would not find it.

What does CONCEALED mean?
explanation: Maya put the present where her brother would not find it, so concealed means hid.

stem: In which sentence does TRUNK mean the long nose of an elephant?
choices: We packed our bags in the trunk of the car.
A squirrel ran up the trunk of the oak tree.
Grandma keeps old photos in a wooden trunk.
The elephant lifted the log with its trunk.
explanation: Only the first sentence is about an elephant using its nose. The others use trunk to mean part of a car, part of a tree, or a large box.

stem:
Please pour the lemonade from the PITCHER into everyone's cups.

What does PITCHER mean in this sentence?
choices: a baseball player who throws the ball
a container with a handle for pouring
explanation: Lemonade is poured from a pitcher, so here it means a container for pouring, not a baseball player.

stem:
When Nora found out she had won the art contest, she was ON CLOUD NINE all week.

What does "on cloud nine" mean?
explanation: Being "on cloud nine" is an idiom that means feeling extremely happy, which fits winning a contest.

stem:
We were planning a surprise party for Dad, but my little brother LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG.

What does this idiom mean?
explanation: To "let the cat out of the bag" means to tell a secret, so Dad found out about the surprise.

stem:
Mom said we could not buy the giant TV because it COSTS AN ARM AND A LEG.

What does this idiom mean?
choices: It is very heavy to carry.
It is too big for the room.
explanation: "Costs an arm and a leg" is an idiom that means something costs a lot of money.

stem: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
choices: The fresh snow was as white as a sheet.
The fresh snow was a white blanket on the field.
The fresh snow fell all night long.
We built a snowman in the fresh snow.
explanation: A metaphor compares two things without using "like" or "as." The snow is called a white blanket. The second choice is a simile because it uses "as."

stem: Which sentence uses personification?
choices: The thunder grumbled angrily across the sky.
The thunder was very loud last night.
We heard thunder after the lightning.
explanation: Personification gives human actions or feelings to things that are not human. Thunder cannot really grumble angrily like a person.

stem:

PUPPY is to DOG as CALF is to ___.
explanation: A puppy is a baby dog, and a calf is a baby cow.

stem:
Complete the analogy.

BIRD is to NEST as BEE is to ___.
explanation: A bird lives in a nest, and a bee lives in a hive.

stem:
The principal will ANNOUNCE the winner of the art contest over the loudspeaker.

What does ANNOUNCE mean?
explanation: Something said over the loudspeaker is told to everyone, so announce means to tell everyone publicly.

stem:
The writing on the old map was so FAINT that we could barely read the names of the towns.

What does FAINT mean?
explanation: If you can barely read the writing, it is hard to see, so faint means not clear or hard to see.

stem:
My swimsuit was still DAMP from the morning, so I hung it in the sun to dry.

Which word means the SAME as DAMP?
explanation: The swimsuit needed to dry, so damp means slightly wet.

stem:
Choose the word that means the OPPOSITE of TEMPORARY.

We lived in a TEMPORARY apartment for two months while our house was being fixed.
explanation: Temporary means lasting only a short time. Its opposite is permanent, which means lasting for a very long time or forever.

stem:
The museum guide will ACCOMPANY our class through the dinosaur hall and answer our questions.

What does ACCOMPANY mean?
explanation: The guide will walk through the hall with the class, so accompany means to go along with.

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

One of my shoes ___ missing.
explanation: The subject is "one," which is singular, so the singular verb "is" is correct.

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

The kittens in the basket ___ sleeping soundly.
explanation: The subject is "kittens," which is plural. The phrase "in the basket" does not change the subject, so use "are."

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

My brother and I ___ going to the library after school.
explanation: "My brother and I" is a plural subject joined by "and," so the plural verb "are" is correct.

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

Last weekend, Carlos ___ his first fish at the lake.
explanation: "Last weekend" shows the past. The past tense of the irregular verb catch is "caught."

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

Yesterday, the school bell ___ ten minutes early.
explanation: The past tense of the irregular verb ring is "rang." "Rung" needs a helping verb, as in "has rung."

stem:
Choose the verbs that best complete the sentence.

I ___ that movie three times already.
explanation: The word "already" goes with the present perfect, and "I" takes "have." The correct form is "have seen."

stem: Which sentence is written in the future tense?
choices: Next summer, we will visit our cousins in Texas.
Last summer, we visited our cousins in Texas.
We are visiting our cousins in Texas now.
We visit our cousins in Texas every summer.
explanation: The helping verb "will" shows an action that has not happened yet, so the first sentence is in the future tense.

stem:
Choose the verb that best completes the sentence.

Every morning, Grandpa ___ the newspaper and drinks his tea.
explanation: The sentence tells about something that happens every morning, and "drinks" is in the present tense, so "reads" keeps the tense the same.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The coach gave ___ students a high five after the game.
explanation: "Us" is the object pronoun that goes with the noun "students" here. You would say "the coach gave us a high five."

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The puppy barked when it saw ___ in the mirror.
explanation: The puppy is called "it," so the reflexive pronoun is "itself."

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Is this umbrella ___? It has your name on it.
explanation: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun that can stand alone. Possessive pronouns never use an apostrophe.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Today is the ___ day of the summer so far.
explanation: When comparing more than two things, use the superlative. For "hot," double the t and add -est: "hottest."

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

My new puppy is ___ than my old cat.
explanation: Two animals are being compared, so use the comparative form "friendlier." Do not use "more" and -er together.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

My cough was bad yesterday, but today I feel much ___.
explanation: "Better" is the comparative form of good and well. "Gooder" is not a word.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The baby slept ___ in her crib all afternoon.
explanation: The word describes how the baby slept, which is a verb, so you need the adverb "peacefully."

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Aisha practiced every day, so she played the violin very ___ at the concert.
explanation: "Well" is an adverb that tells how she played. "Good" is an adjective and should describe a noun.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

Hurry up, ___ you will miss the bus!
explanation: Here "or" means "if not": if you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

We will move the picnic inside ___ it starts to rain.
explanation: "If" shows a condition: the picnic moves inside only when it rains. "Unless" would mean the opposite of what makes sense.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

We have lived in this town ___ 2019.
explanation: Use "since" with a starting point in time, such as a year. "For" is used with an amount of time, like "for five years."

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

My baby sister was born ___ May.
explanation: Use "in" with months and years. Use "on" with specific days, such as "on May 3."

stem: Which of these is a sentence fragment?
choices: The ducks swam under the bridge.
explanation: "Under the old wooden bridge" has no subject and no verb, so it does not express a complete thought.

stem:

Mia likes apples. Mia likes pears.
choices: Mia likes apples, Mia likes pears.
Mia likes apples, and pears, Mia likes.
explanation: Both sentences have the same subject and verb, so you can join the two objects with "and": "Mia likes apples and pears."

stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
choices: For our picnic we packed, sandwiches apples and juice.
For our picnic, we packed sandwiches apples, and juice.
For our, picnic we packed sandwiches, apples and, juice.
For our picnic, we packed sandwiches, apples, and juice.
explanation: Commas separate the items in a list and set off the introductory phrase "For our picnic."

stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
choices: On June, 5 2024 our class planted a tree.
On June 5 2024, our class, planted a tree.
On June 5, 2024, our class planted a tree.
On, June 5, 2024 our class planted a tree.
explanation: A comma goes between the day and the year, and another comma follows the year when the date begins the sentence.

stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
choices: The girls bike's has a flat tire.
The girl's bike has a flat tire.
The girl's bike's has a flat tire.
The girls' bike has a flat tire's.
explanation: One girl owns the bike, so the apostrophe goes before the s in "girl's." The word "bike" is not possessive and needs no apostrophe.

stem: Which word is the correct contraction for "will not"?
explanation: "Won't" is the special contraction for "will not."

stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
choices: On thursday, we ate dinner with aunt Lisa for Thanksgiving.
On Thursday, we ate Dinner with Aunt Lisa for thanksgiving.
on Thursday, we ate dinner with Aunt lisa for Thanksgiving.
On Thursday, we ate dinner with Aunt Lisa for Thanksgiving.
explanation: Days of the week, holidays, and names with titles (Aunt Lisa) are capitalized. Common nouns like "dinner" are not.

stem:
Choose the word that best completes the sentence.

The dentist cleaned all of my ___.
explanation: "Tooth" has an irregular plural form: "teeth."

stem:
Which word in this sentence is an adverb?

The children laughed loudly at the silly clown.
explanation: "Loudly" tells how the children laughed, so it is an adverb. "Silly" is an adjective that describes the clown.

stem: Which sentence should end with a question mark?
choices: Please put my book on the shelf
I put the book on the shelf
Where did you put my library book
What a great book this is
explanation: "Where did you put my library book" asks a question, so it needs a question mark. The others are a command, a statement, and an exclamation.
